item.title: Guam voters point to cost of living, education and public safety as key election concerns
item.description: Guam voters headed to the polls Tuesday with concerns about the island's cost of living, education, public safety, and the future decisions in this year's general election. In interviews with KPRG News at polling locations across the island, residents shared what motivated them to vote and what they hope the island's next elected leaders will address.
item.content:encoded:
Guam voters headed to the polls Tuesday with concerns about the island's cost of living, education, public safety, and the future decisions in this year's general election.

In interviews with KPRG News at polling locations across the island, residents shared what motivated them to vote and what they hope the island's next elected leaders will address.

For some, rising living expenses remain a major concern. Voters pointed to increasing housing costs, rent and utility bills, along with the need for more employment opportunities and livable wages.

Yona resident Evan San Nicolas said balancing employment and household expenses remains a challenge, regardless of whether someone works in the public, private, or nonprofit sector.

“Some important issues to me are the cost of living,” San Nicolas said. “Ultimately, I am a homeowner, so also tying in employment. Seeing, are we able to find a good job? In every sector of employment, it is such a task to be qualified for it, and the timing of everything too, also blends in towards when our bills are due, that kind of thing.”

Education was another recurring concern, particularly among parents who said the island's children depend on stronger support for schools and teachers.

Cherish Keaunui said her children were her primary motivation for voting. She also raised concerns about the lack of support for teachers and the rising costs of basic living expenses.

“Education is a really big thing. With the lack in support that I’ve seen for teachers, that’s what really pushed me,” Keaunui said. “And then also today with like a lot of the rising costs and living, you know, rent, utilities and stuff, it’s been a big burden. And I know its a big thing on everybody. But today, I really needed to vote because my kids rely on it.”

Public safety and drug abuse were also among the issues voters want the next administration to address.

Mark Alviz said he wants to see greater attention given to the island's safety, including efforts to address Guam's drug problem. “I mean, just how it’s gotten just so bad over the last how many years, just there needs to be change there,” Alviz said. He also expressed concern about Guam's strategic position as a military location and the importance of having leaders who prioritize the island's security. “So I just want to make sure when voting, having the right people that put that as a priority is one quality that I’m looking for,” Alviz said.

Other residents raised concerns about government services and accountability.

Vince Flores of Agana Heights pointed to challenges facing the education system and hospital, as well as government spending, procurement, and transparency. He said the government needs to find ways to improve services and create more opportunities for residents to own businesses and build their livelihoods on Guam.

“The important issues are education, the education process, and the system right now is always hurting,” Flores said. “It’s like, how is that happening? And other services within the agencies, and we just have too much overhead. They got to think outside the box and provide some assistance somehow, someway.”

For some voters, the election also carried concerns about the future of the island's indigenous population.

Dededo resident and veteran Joe Leon Guerrero said he hopes more CHamoru people will remain on Guam or return home to support their communities. He expressed concern about residents leaving the island and the need to ensure the local population continues to thrive.

“The reason why I’m voting is because our people are dying out and leaving the island,” Leon Guerrero said. “Outsiders are coming in, and one day they’re going to take over if people keep neglecting from voting. So please vote.”

While voters identified different priorities, their responses reflected a shared expectation that the island's next leaders address the challenges affecting residents' everyday lives.

As Guam begins its next election cycle, voters say casting their ballots is one way to make their voices heard on the issues that matter to them.

item.title: CNMI voters head to polls as 2026 general election begins

According to the Commonwealth Election Commission, 18,521 voters are registered for the 2026 general election. The commission reported that 5,417 ballots
item.content:encoded:
Voters across the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands headed to the polls Tuesday as the 2026 general election got underway, with more than 5,400 ballots already cast through early voting and several high-profile races set to be decided.

According to the Commonwealth Election Commission, 18,521 voters are registered for the 2026 general election. The commission reported that 5,417 ballots had been cast through early voting as of Sunday.

Polls remained open throughout the day as voters on Saipan, Tinian and Rota selected candidates for governor and lieutenant governor, delegate to the U.S. House of Representatives, attorney general and legislative seats across the commonwealth.

In addition to candidate races, voters are deciding whether to convene a constitutional convention to propose amendments to the CNMI Constitution.

The proposal has attracted significant public attention because it could open the door to changes affecting the structure and operation of government and other constitutional provisions.

According to the Northern Mariana Islands Bar Association, a "yes" vote supports holding a constitutional convention to propose amendments, while a "no" vote opposes convening a convention.

The question faces a higher threshold than most ballot measures. For it to pass, at least two-thirds of all votes cast on the constitutional convention question commonwealthwide must be in favor. A simple majority is not enough.

The Commonwealth Election Commission is also prepared to conduct runoff elections if necessary. Under CNMI law, a runoff election is required if no gubernatorial ticket or attorney general candidate receives more than half of all votes cast and counted in the general election.

Any runoff election would be held 14 days after the Commonwealth Election Commission certifies the election results.

The possibility of a runoff has added another layer of interest to the gubernatorial and attorney general contests, particularly if multiple candidates divide the vote and prevent any contender from securing an outright majority.

Election officials are expected to begin releasing results after voting concludes Tuesday evening. Attention will focus on turnout, the outcomes of the commonwealth's major races and whether voters approve the constitutional convention question by the required two-thirds margin.

item.title: Guam voters head to the polls Tuesday
item.description: Guam voters will go to the polls Tuesday to select a new gubernatorial team, congressional delegate, attorney general and senators. Other races on the ballot include the Consolidated Commission on Utilities and the Guam Board of Education.
item.content:encoded:
Guam voters will go to the polls Tuesday to select a new gubernatorial team, congressional delegate, attorney general and senators.

Other races on the ballot include the Consolidated Commission on Utilities and the Guam Board of Education.

Republicans Tony Ada and E.J. Calvo are running for governor and lieutenant governor against Democrats Therese Terlaje and Sabina Perez.

In the race for Guam’s non-voting congressional delegate, Democrat Alicia Limtiaco is challenging Republican incumbent James Moylan.

There are 15 Republicans running for the legislature, including seven incumbents, and 15 Democrats, including two incumbents.

Five candidates, including incumbent Doug Moylan, are running for the Office of the Attorney General. Challengers are Phillip Tydingco, Jordan Paulhun, Thomas Fisher and Peter Santos.

Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. To find your precinct’s voting location, or to review a sample ballot, visit the Guam Election Commission website at gec.guam.gov .

item.title: Death toll hits 29 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with 48 still missing

item.content:encoded:
KYIV, Ukraine — The death toll from a Russian attack in southern Ukraine on a site where people had gathered to receive humanitarian aid rose to 29 on Tuesday, with 48 still missing, as a wave of overnight strikes targeted power plants across the country, damaged hospitals and wounded scores of people.

Dozens of rescuers and volunteers continued to search the cratered blast site of a destroyed aid facility and shelter in Komyushuvakha, a village in Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia region, hoping to find missing residents alive under the rubble. Instead, more bodies were pulled out and carried away in white plastic sheeting.

"The scale of the tragedy is terrifying," Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of the region's military administration, wrote in an online post. "This is one of the worst tragedies in terms of the number of civilian victims in our region since the start of the full-scale war."

Russia launched 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles across nine regions, triggering emergency power cuts, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an online post that noted the barrage coincided with U.S. elections.

"The Russians think America won't notice this signal of theirs," he said. "But we need to notice and stop such terror. We need to help Ukraine defend its skies; otherwise, Russia will never stop its missile strikes."

Three days of mourning were declared in Zaporizhzhia where Russian bunker-busting bombs, filled with nearly 1.5 tons of explosives, were used in Monday's attack.

The dead included four police officers and two rescue workers, Semikin said Tuesday. At least five people were hurt.

In the northeast region of Kharkiv, a combined Russian missile and drone attack wounded at least 62 people, local authorities said.

A strike damaged a medical facility in the Nemyshlianskyi district, shattered windows in four apartment buildings and damaged cars. More than 200 patients were transferred to other medical facilities, head of the regional military administration Oleh Syniehubov said.

In the Dnipro area, rescuers pulled a woman alive from the rubble Tuesday morning, after a Russian attack killed one person and wounded 17, local authorities said.

The attack damaged an outpatient clinic and a hospital. Patients were transferred to other hospitals, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Tuesday that it had shot down 856 Ukrainian drones overnight. Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 493 drones were fired toward the Russian capital.

A Ukrainian drone attack wounded two employees at an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl, regional Gov. Mikhail Yevrayev said Tuesday. He added that there was damage to the refinery's infrastructure.

Rolling blackouts have been instituted in the south, west and east of Russian-occupied Crimea following attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow-installed officials said Tuesday.

item.title: Four types of House races to watch on election night to know how it might go

item.content:encoded:
Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrats appear poised to retake control of the House on Tuesday. If they do, will their majority be built upon a blue wave or a tiny trickle? A previous NPR analysis found both parties spending deep and wide in a competitive landscape that spans 70 districts, ranging from longtime tossups to newly-competitive seats in deeply conservative areas.

Republicans came into Election Day with a narrow 218-214 seat advantage in the House and facing severe headwinds as the party in power. This midterm cycle has also seen a record number of departures from Congress , and polls show voters aren't happy about things like the economy and the ongoing war in Iran.

So what separates a good night for Democrats from a blue wave that sees dozens of House seats change hands? Here's NPR's cheat sheet to four types of House races to watch as results come in:

The first results of the night with national implications will likely be from Kentucky's 5th Congressional District ( KY-06 ) and Indiana's 5th ( IN-5 ), two districts where polls close first (in the 6 p.m. ET hour) and whose 2024 margins for President Trump (15 and 17 points, respectively) could act as a preview for how much voters have soured on Republicans.

Democrats and Republicans alike have spent heavily in the Kentucky race, where Democrat Zach Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado, so the increased investment is worth noting as a factor on the outcome. If Democrats flip one or both of these races, then it will likely be a long night for the GOP.

Florida also counts and reports its votes quickly, and is home to more than a half dozen races that are viewed as toss-ups or slightly favor one party or the other, so as these districts have projected winners there will be more insight into other races across the country.

Like the Kentucky contest, both parties have spent significant sums in races like the open seat in FL-22 with Democrat Pia Dandiya facing off against Republican Casey Askar and incumbent Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz versus Republican Scott Singer in the newly-redrawn FL-25 race.

Other races to watch: FL-27, NC-11, SC-01, VA-01

In the final seven days of the midterms, a handful of House races have seen more than $10 million in ad spending, according to data from AdImpact. It's a sign of where both parties think the saying "It all comes down to turnout!" is more than a cliche. That includes districts in Michigan, such as MI-07 , where progressive Democrat William Lawrence is challenging incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in a seat that Trump carried by just over one percent in 2024 and the open MI-10 , where Democrat Christina Hines faces Republican Mike Bouchard.

New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in NY-17 could be one of the rare Republicans who holds on to his seat thanks in part to his party's ad spending advantage in the closing stretch against Democrat Cait Conley.

Three of Iowa's four House races, IA-01, IA-02 and IA-03 are on the list of most expensive, in part because of the competitive governor and U.S. Senate races that are also on the ballot and driving up turnout.

Other races to watch: CO-08, PA-01, WA-03, WI-03

This year's Supreme Court decision rolling back part of the Voting Rights Act led to many Republican-led states redrawing their House maps to eliminate districts that favor Democrats in a typical election year – but this year is not typical.

Now, the political environment has deteriorated so much that seats like AL-02, held by Democrat Shomari Figures, OH-09 held by Democrat Marcy Kaptur and NC-01 held by Democrat Don Davis are all considered toss-ups at best and favoring the Democrats at worst for Republicans.

In Texas, Latino voters seem poised to swing back to Democratic candidates and could prevent Republican Eric Flores from flipping the seat held by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in TX-34 or Tano Tijerina from unseating Democratic incumbent Henry Cuellar in TX-28 .

Other races to watch: CA-22, FL-09, FL-14, TX-35

As results continue to be reported, one thing to watch is how far into conservative communities the increased support for Democrats can go.

One race that has received a surprising amount of ad attention is in Arkansas's 2nd district ( AR-02) , where incumbent Republican Rep. French Hill faces a well-known challenger in Democrat Chris Jones. By the time polls close, closer to $10 million will have been spent in the final months on the Little Rock-based seat that Trump carried by 15 points in 2024.

There are also many districts in states that redrew their maps where the Republican gerrymander could backfire, like Ohio. In both OH-10 held by Republican Mike Turner and OH-15 held by Republican Mike Carey, Trump won by closer to 10 points in 2024. They're also in a state with competitive governor and Senate races and stretch between the suburbs and exurbs of Dayton and Columbus with an electorate that could swing away from the GOP.

The margin in North Carolina's Senate race, where former Gov. Roy Cooper is expected to win against former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, could determine if races like NC-03 are in play as well too. Rep. Greg Murphy's district absorbed more Democratic-leaning voters after the latest map redraw.

Other races to watch: NC-09, NY-21 TN-09, WA-05

item.title: New restrictions at Texas Tech are changing what professors can teach
item.description: LUBBOCK, Texas — Outside the library at Texas Tech University on a recent Wednesday morning, a small group gathered behind a folding table in a spot known to students as the "free speech area." Spread across the table flyers referenced names of familiar works.
item.content:encoded:
LUBBOCK, Texas — Outside the library at Texas Tech University on a recent Wednesday morning, a small group gathered behind a folding table in a spot known to students as the "free speech area."

Spread across the table flyers referenced names of familiar works.

Homer's The Odyssey . William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet . Herman Melville's Moby-Dick .

Students streamed past on their way to and from class. Most kept walking. Every so often, someone lingered long enough to ask what the list was about.

The people behind the table were Texas Tech professors. And the works printed on those flyers were examples of texts that professors say could run afoul of new rules governing what they can teach.

Texas Tech is among the state's 45 public universities navigating a wave of higher education policy changes. That shift began with Senate Bill 17 , the 2023 law banning diversity, equity and inclusion offices and programs at public universities, while explicitly exempting classroom instruction and academic research. More changes followed in 2025, including new state oversight of university curriculum.

Texas Tech has since adopted some of the state's most sweeping restrictions on how professors can teach about race, sex, gender identity and sexual orientation. The rules have led to changes in course materials, prompted accusations of censorship and fueled pushback from faculty and students.

Deena Varner, an assistant professor of practice in English who's taught at Texas Tech for five years, was among the professors who stood in the Texas heat talking with students about how the new rules could affect the courses they take.

Varner said she and her colleagues have spoken with hundreds of students since they began tabling nine months ago, continuing even after university administrators instructed faculty not to discuss the new policies with students.

Inside the classroom, professors face the uncertainty of what's allowed to be taught.

"Everyone is walking around really afraid of doing the wrong thing, saying the wrong thing, teaching the wrong thing," Varner said. "Because everyone has a gender identity and everyone has sexual orientation, what it means to not be able to talk about those things is really unclear."

And the consequences for getting it wrong can be significant. Texas Tech administrators have warned that faculty who don't comply with the new policies could face disciplinary action.

"It's a scary time," Varner said. "One of the things that I try to tell myself every morning is that I have rights and it's my civic duty to exercise my rights, and that's one of the things that kind of keeps me going."

The restrictions began taking shape shortly after Brandon Creighton became chancellor of the Texas Tech University System in November 2025.

During his first five months on the job, Creighton issued two directives — one in December 2025 and another in April 2026 — outlining what could be taught across the system.

Together, the policies restrict how professors can teach about race, sex, sexual orientation and gender identity. They also call for phasing out academic programs centered on those topics.

Before becoming chancellor, Creighton spent more than a decade in the Texas Senate where he chaired the higher education committee. He authored SB 17 in 2023, and two years later, he spearheaded Senate Bill 37 , which gave university governing boards greater authority over curriculum and required regular reviews of core courses.

An earlier version would have barred core courses from teaching "identity politics" or theories that systemic racism, sexism, oppression or privilege are inherent in U.S. institutions. Lawmakers removed that language before the bill passed.

The final law, instead, prohibits core courses from requiring students to adopt beliefs that one race, sex, ethnicity, or social, political or religious belief is inherently superior to another.

After becoming chancellor, however, Creighton imposed restrictions at Texas Tech on some of the same subjects lawmakers had removed from his bill.

Creighton's office and the Texas Tech University System Board of Regents did not respond to multiple requests for comment on this story.

Creighton has described the law as a "floor" for what Texas Tech can do, signaling that the system's policies could go further than what the Legislature required. He has also pushed back on some groups of professors and students describing the restrictions as censorship.

"I think that it's easy to throw those types of terms around, but at the end of the day, we have to make decisions, and decisions that are centered around what is best for our students and the future workforce that we see on the horizon," Creighton said in an April interview with Everything Lubbock. "I think that it's appropriate."

Creighton has found support among some conservative students . In August, Preston Parsons, president of Texas Tech's Turning Point USA chapter, described the policies as a return to "biblical truth." Parsons declined an NPR request for an interview.

Across Texas Tech, professors say the restrictions are changing what they can bring into the classroom, from the books they assign to the subjects they discuss and even material drawn from their own research.

Varner said she was pressured to remove course material involving "The Silence of the Lambs" because its villain, Buffalo Bill, could be interpreted as transgender.

"I tend to teach about structures of power, and that often includes relationships related to gender, sexuality, race, class, ethnicity, so it impacts me directly quite a bit," Varner said.

Paul Ingram, an associate professor of psychology at Texas Tech, said the restrictions have affected how he teaches about suicide, including discussion of differences in suicide risk among men and women. He said the policies have created a conflict between following university rules and giving students the level of training he believes the science demands.

"I think that hurts Texas Tech. I think it hurts my career. I think it hurts my students. I think it hurts education," Ingram said. "It hurts the mission of this university."

The effects aren't always as visible as a book or lesson being explicitly removed. Faculty members say uncertainty over where the university draws the line has led some professors to avoid certain subjects altogether — resulting in what they describe as self-censorship.
